summary: Supply the inside railing distance, the spindle width, the maximum allowable spacing and the effective tread run and the Spindle spacing calculator solves for riser rise. It suits a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Spindle spacing calculator work?
sections.html:
The Spindle spacing calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports riser rise in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the spacing option); then you type in the inside railing distance, the spindle width, the maximum allowable spacing and the effective tread run.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Spindle spacing calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Riser rise=effective tread run × the tangent of (stair pitch)
Number of spindles=rounded up, ((inside railing distance + spindle width) ÷ (maximum allowable spacing + spindle width)) − 1
Spindle-to-spindle spacing=(maximum allowable spacing × rounded up, (1 ÷ 1000000))
End spacing=-1 ÷ 2 × maximum allowable spacing × rounded up, ((inside railing distance + spindle width) ÷ (maximum allowable spacing + spindle width)) + maximum allowable spacing + (1 ÷ 2) × inside railing distance − 1 ÷ 2 × spindle width × rounded up, ((inside railing distance + spindle width) ÷ (maximum allowable spacing + spindle width)) + (1 ÷ 2) × spindle width
Slanted end spacing=((1 ÷ 2) × (-maximum allowable spacing × rounded down, (inside railing distance ÷ (maximum allowable spacing + spindle width)) − maximum allowable spacing × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 2) × rounded up, (-rounded down, (inside railing distance ÷ (maximum allowable spacing + spindle width)) + inside railing distance ÷ maximum allowable spacing − spindle width × rounded down, (inside railing distance ÷ (maximum allowable spacing + spindle width)) ÷ maximum allowable spacing)) + maximum allowable spacing + inside railing distance − spindle width × rounded down, (inside railing distance ÷ (maximum allowable spacing + spindle width)) − spindle width × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 2) × rounded up, (-rounded down, (inside railing distance ÷ (maximum allowable spacing + spindle width)) + inside railing distance ÷ maximum allowable spacing − spindle width × rounded down, (inside railing distance ÷ (maximum allowable spacing + spindle width)) ÷ maximum allowable spacing))) ÷ the cosine of (stair pitch))
Slanted spindle-to-spindle spacing=(maximum allowable spacing ÷ the cosine of (stair pitch))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Calculate spindle spacing for set to A deck, Spacing option set to Evenly-spaced spindles, Maximum allowable spacing = 10 cm and Effective tread run = 30 cm. Working through the relationship above gives Riser rise = 5.2898 cm and Slanted spindle-to-spindle spacing = 10.154 cm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Riser rise = 5.2898 cm and Slanted spindle-to-spindle spacing = 10.154 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Calculate spindle spacing for set to A deck and Spacing option set to Evenly-spaced spindles.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in centimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Spindle spacing calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the inside railing distance, the spindle width and the maximum allowable spacing — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Spindle spacing calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns riser rise, derived from the inside railing distance, the spindle width and the maximum allowable spacing. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Spindle spacing calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the inside railing distance, the spindle width, the maximum allowable spacing and the effective tread run, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter inside railing distance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Inside railing distance opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Riser rise = 5.2898 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Spindle spacing calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
